chapter.name: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

questions.q: A lab assistant finds an unlabelled bottle. A strip of blue litmus dipped in it stays blue and a strip of red litmus stays red. The bottle could contain
questions.a: No change in either paper means the liquid is neutral. Sugar solution is neutral; vinegar is acidic; lime water and washing powder solution are basic.
o: sugar solution
vinegar
lime water
washing powder solution

questions.q: Four liquids were tested. W turns blue litmus red. X changes neither red nor blue litmus. Y turns red litmus blue. For Z only blue litmus was used, and it did not change. Name the nature of W, X and Y, say what can and cannot be concluded about Z, and name the test that settles it.
questions.a: W acidic, X neutral, Y basic. Z is not acidic, but it may be basic or neutral. Test Z with red litmus: blue means basic, no change means neutral.
s: W acidic, X neutral, Y basic
Z is not acidic but could be basic or neutral
Red litmus test settles it

questions.q:
At the school science fair, Ritu tests four colourless liquids P, Q, R and T with litmus. P turns blue litmus red and leaves red litmus unchanged. Q turns red litmus blue. R changes neither litmus paper. For liquid T she has only a red litmus strip, and it did not change.
(a) State the nature of P, Q and R.
(b) Name one sample from the chapter that behaves like P and one that behaves like R.
(c) Which of P and Q would you expect to feel slippery between the fingers?
(d) Can Ritu decide the nature of T from her result? State what she should do.
questions.a: (a) P acidic, Q basic, R neutral. (b) P: lemon juice (or amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar); R: tap water, sugar solution or salt solution. (c) Q, because bases generally feel slippery. (d) No: red litmus does not change in acidic or neutral liquids, so T could be either; she should test T with blue litmus.
s: Part (a): P acidic, Q basic, R neutral
Part (b): a correct acidic and a correct neutral sample
Part (c): Q feels slippery
Part (d): cannot decide, uses blue litmus

questions.q: Write a table of observations (colour of blue litmus, colour of red litmus) that would make three samples respectively acidic, basic and neutral. Name one real sample from the chapter for each.
questions.a: Acidic: blue becomes red, red unchanged (lemon juice). Basic: blue unchanged, red becomes blue (soap solution). Neutral: both unchanged (salt solution).
s: Acidic row with correct colours and a sample
Basic row with correct colours and a sample
Neutral row with correct colours and a sample

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Baking soda solution turns red litmus paper blue.
Reason (R): Baking soda solution feels soapy or slippery between the fingers.
questions.a: Both are true, but the slippery feel is only a property of bases; it is not the reason red litmus turns blue.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q: Dhruv says: 'A liquid that turns blue litmus red is acidic, so I need not test it with red litmus.' Do you agree? Give a reason.
questions.a: Yes. Only acidic substances turn blue litmus red, so the result already shows the liquid is acidic. Red litmus would not change in an acid, so it adds no new information.
s: Verdict: agrees
Reason: only acids turn blue litmus red
Red litmus gives no new information here

questions.q:
Manoj makes lime water for the science fair stall by mixing a spoonful of chuna in a glass of water, leaving it for an hour and filtering the clear liquid. He also has lemon juice and tap water. He can test visitors' samples with blue and red litmus papers, or spend ten minutes preparing red rose extract and then use one test only.
(a) Name the compound in chuna and the compound dissolved in lime water.
(b) What will red litmus and red rose extract show with lime water?
(c) Can blue litmus alone separate lime water, lemon juice and tap water? Can red litmus alone? Does the extract?
(d) The stall expects a long queue. Choose papers or extract and justify with a trade-off.
questions.a: (a) Chuna is calcium oxide; lime water contains calcium hydroxide. (b) Red litmus turns blue; the extract turns green; lime water is basic. (c) Blue litmus alone: only lemon juice turns red, lime water and tap water look alike. Red litmus alone: only lime water turns blue, the other two look alike. The extract gives three different results (green, red, no change). (d) Either choice is acceptable if justified: papers are ready at once but need two tests per sample; the extract takes ten minutes to prepare but one test per sample separates all three.
s: Part (a): calcium oxide and calcium hydroxide
Part (b): red litmus turns blue, extract turns green
Part (c): neither paper alone separates all three, the extract does
Part (d): a choice backed by the trade-off of time against number of tests

questions.q: Meena says: 'Sour means acid and bitter means base, so tasting is the best way to test any liquid.' Justify why this is not a good method, using facts from the chapter.
questions.a: Sour taste does suggest an acid in edible substances such as lemon juice. Bases generally taste bitter, but bitter gourd is bitter without being basic, so taste can mislead. Unknown substances must never be tasted. Litmus gives a clear colour change in acids and bases. So litmus is the safe, reliable test.
s: Sour edible substances tend to be acidic
Bitter is not a sure sign of a base: bitter gourd
Unknown substances must never be tasted
Litmus gives a clear colour result
Conclusion: use an indicator, not taste

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A liquid that leaves blue litmus unchanged must be basic.
2. Litmus is a natural substance obtained from lichens.
3. Soap solution turns red litmus paper blue.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are true. 1 is false: a neutral liquid also leaves blue litmus unchanged.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Gurbir has three unlabelled bottles: tamarind water, washing powder solution and salt solution. He has only red and blue litmus paper, a tile and a dropper. Describe how he can name each bottle, giving the observation expected in each case.
questions.a: Put a drop from each bottle on blue litmus. Tamarind water turns it red, so it is acidic. The other two leave blue litmus unchanged, so test them on red litmus. Washing powder solution turns red litmus blue, so it is basic. Salt solution changes neither paper, so it is neutral.
s: Uses a separate drop of each bottle on litmus (blue litmus first, or red litmus first is equally valid)
Tamarind water: acidic, blue litmus turns red
Remaining two tested on the other litmus paper
Washing powder solution: basic, red litmus turns blue
Salt solution: neutral, no change on either paper

questions.q: Gurbir says lime water is the same as the juice of a lime. Explain how lime water is actually prepared and why he is wrong.
questions.a: Mix chuna (calcium oxide) in water, leave about an hour and filter; the clear liquid is lime water, a solution of calcium hydroxide. Lime is a fruit similar to lemon.
s: Preparation: chuna in water, left to stand, filtered
Lime is a fruit like lemon, not the same as lime water

questions.q: A student claims a solution turned blue litmus red and red litmus blue at the same time. Show why this cannot be a single correct observation.
questions.a: Turning blue litmus red means the solution is acidic; turning red litmus blue means it is basic. A solution cannot be both acidic and basic, so one observation must be wrong (or two liquids were mixed).
s: Blue litmus turning red shows acidic
Red litmus turning blue shows basic
A single solution cannot be both, so the claim fails

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the conclusion in Column II.
Column I: 1. Blue litmus turns red and red litmus is unchanged; 2. Red litmus turns blue and blue litmus is unchanged; 3. Both papers stay as they were; 4. The liquid tastes bitter but both papers stay as they were
Column II: a. Basic, like washing powder solution; b. Neutral, like salt solution; c. Acidic, like amla juice; d. Bitter taste alone does not make a substance basic (karela)

On a rainy-season trip to a hill town, Rhea sees a crusty grey-green growth on a tree trunk. Her teacher calls it a lichen and says litmus comes from such growths. Which statement about the lichen and litmus is correct?
questions.a: A lichen is formed by the association of a fungus and an alga; litmus is a natural substance obtained from lichens (synthetic indicators are a separate group made in laboratories).
o: The lichen is a fungus and an alga living together, and litmus is a natural substance obtained from it
The lichen is a single green plant, and litmus is a synthetic substance made from it in a laboratory
The lichen is a fungus living alone, and litmus is obtained from its flowers and petals
The lichen is two algae living together, and litmus is obtained from turmeric roots

questions.q: (a) A drop of vinegar is put on blue litmus paper and a drop of baking soda solution on red litmus paper. State the colour change in each. (b) Which of the two samples would feel slippery between the fingers, and why can taste alone not settle that a liquid is basic?
questions.a: (a) Vinegar turns blue litmus red; baking soda solution turns red litmus blue. (b) Baking soda solution (a base) feels slippery. Bitter taste cannot settle it because bitter gourd (karela) tastes bitter but is not basic.
s: (a) Vinegar blue to red; baking soda red to blue
(b) Baking soda feels slippery; karela is bitter but not basic

questions.q: True or False: 'Red litmus paper stays red in vinegar, so vinegar is neutral.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Red litmus stays red in acidic as well as neutral liquids. Vinegar is acidic and only blue litmus (turning red) reveals that.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: red litmus is unchanged by acids too, so blue litmus is needed

questions.q: Ayaan records the results of four unlabelled liquids on a tile. P: blue litmus turns red. Q: red litmus turns blue. R: neither paper changes. S: neither paper changes. Which set of names fits P, Q, R and S in that order?
questions.a: P is acidic (lemon juice), Q is basic (soap solution), R and S are neutral (tap water, sugar solution). The wrong sets put a neutral or basic liquid where an acid is needed, or two acids in the neutral places.
o: Lemon juice, soap solution, tap water, sugar solution
Tap water, soap solution, lemon juice, vinegar
Soap solution, lemon juice, tap water, salt solution
Lemon juice, lime water, vinegar, sugar solution

questions.q: Asha's blue litmus turns red in a liquid, Bela's red litmus stays red in the same liquid, and Chandra's turmeric paper stays yellow in it. The liquid is ___ in nature.
questions.a: acidic

questions.q: Four students describe their kitchen tests. Whose conclusion is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Bitter gourd (karela) tastes bitter but is not basic, so bitterness alone does not prove a base. The other three conclusions follow from the chapter.
o: Neel: karela juice tastes bitter, so it must be basic
Pia: baking soda solution feels slippery, so I expect it to turn red litmus blue
Qadir: amla juice tastes sour, so I expect it to turn blue litmus red
Rina: lime water comes from chuna kept in water and filtered, not from squeezing a fruit

questions.q: Differentiate between acidic and basic substances on the basis of (a) action on litmus and (b) feel or taste.
questions.a: Acidic: turn blue litmus red; taste sour. Basic: turn red litmus blue; generally bitter and soapy or slippery.
s: Litmus action of each given correctly
Taste or feel of each given correctly

questions.q: Farhan puts one drop of amla juice on a piece of blue litmus paper and another drop on a piece of red litmus paper. What will he observe?
questions.a: Amla juice is acidic: it turns blue litmus red and leaves red litmus unchanged.
o: The blue paper turns red; the red paper does not change.
The blue paper does not change; the red paper turns blue.
Both papers turn red.
Neither paper changes colour.

questions.q:
(a) A sample turns red litmus blue. State its nature.
(b) Name one sample from the chapter that behaves the same way and one that would turn blue litmus red instead.
questions.a: (a) Basic. (b) Basic: soap solution (or baking soda, lime water, washing powder solution). Turns blue litmus red: lemon juice (or amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar).
s: Part (a): basic
Part (b): one basic and one acidic sample named correctly

questions.q: At a hill-town nursery, the owner shakes soil from a hydrangea bed in water, filters it and adds red rose extract. The extract turns red. What flower colour should she expect on the shrubs in that bed?
questions.a: Red extract means the soil is acidic, and acidic soil gives blue hydrangea flowers; pink or red flowers need basic soil. The 'red extract means red flowers' reading is the trap.
o: Blue
Pink or red
Green
No fixed colour; soil has no effect on it

questions.q: Rekha's hydrangea shrub bears blue flowers but she wants pink ones. Which idea should she use?
questions.a: Blue flowers mean acidic soil; pink or red flowers come in basic soil, and lime is a base.
o: Make the soil basic, for example by adding lime
Make the soil more acidic by adding excess chemical fertiliser
Sprinkle lemon juice on the soil every day
Nothing can be done because the colour depends only on the plant

questions.q: Tarun says: 'Soap solution turns red rose extract green, so it will also turn blue litmus paper red.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Green with red rose extract shows the soap solution is basic. A basic solution turns red litmus blue and leaves blue litmus unchanged; blue litmus turns red only in acidic liquids.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Green with the extract means basic
A base turns red litmus blue, not blue litmus red

questions.q: A test tube of red rose extract turns green when liquid X is added. State what you can say about X, name one common sample X could be, and predict what red and blue litmus would show with X.
questions.a: X is basic. It could be soap solution (or lime water, baking soda solution). Red litmus would turn blue; blue litmus would not change.
s: X is basic
A suitable basic sample named
Litmus prediction correct for both papers

questions.q: (a) A gardener's hydrangea bush bears pink flowers. State the likely nature of its soil and the colour that red rose extract would show with the soil water. (b) She wants blue flowers instead. Should she make the soil more acidic or more basic?
questions.a: (a) The soil is basic; the extract turns green. (b) More acidic, since acidic soil gives blue flowers.
s: (a) Basic soil; extract green
(b) Make it more acidic for blue flowers

questions.q: Red rose extract turns red with liquid K, turns green with liquid L and shows no change with liquid M. (a) Name the nature of K, L and M. (b) A student says K and M will both turn blue litmus red. Correct her and say what each does to blue litmus.
questions.a: (a) K acidic, L basic, M neutral. (b) Only K turns blue litmus red; M, being neutral, leaves it unchanged.
s: (a) K acidic, L basic, M neutral
(b) Only K turns blue litmus red; M leaves it unchanged

questions.q: True or False: 'A sample that turns red rose extract red will also turn blue litmus paper red.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The samples that gave a shade of red with the extract were the same as those in the group that turned blue litmus red; both show an acidic nature.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the extract and blue litmus give the same grouping of acidic samples

questions.q: Show why sugar solution cannot turn red rose extract green.
questions.a: Green with the extract means the solution is basic. Sugar solution leaves both litmus papers unchanged, so it is neutral, not basic. Neutral solutions do not change the extract.
s: Green means basic
Sugar solution is neutral (no litmus change)
Neutral solutions leave the extract unchanged

questions.q: Differentiate between litmus and red rose extract on the basis of the colours they show in acidic and basic solutions.
questions.a: Litmus: blue litmus turns red in acids, red litmus turns blue in bases. Red rose extract: red in acids, green in bases.
s: Litmus colour changes correct
Red rose extract colours correct

questions.q: Liquid L turns red rose extract red and liquid M turns it green. The two are mixed in a third tube. State the nature of L and M and the colours the extract could show in the mixture.
questions.a: L is acidic and M is basic. The mixture can show red if acid is left over, green if base is left over, or no change if they exactly neutralise each other.
s: L acidic and M basic
Red or green when one of them is in excess
No change if exactly neutralised

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Red rose extract turns green in soap solution.
2. Red rose extract changes colour in every solution it is added to.
3. The colour of hydrangea flowers depends on the nature of the soil.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are true. 2 is false: neutral solutions leave the extract unchanged.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Priya adds a few drops of red rose extract to soap solution in one test tube and to sugar solution in another. What does she see?
questions.a: Soap solution is basic, so the extract turns green; sugar solution is neutral, so it does not change.
o: Green in soap solution; no change in sugar solution
Red in soap solution; green in sugar solution
Red in soap solution; no change in sugar solution
No colour change in the soap solution or in the sugar solution

questions.q: A hydrangea bed gives blue flowers. Soil water from that bed will turn red rose extract ___ in colour.
questions.a: red

questions.q:
Match each test in Column I with the result in Column II.
Column I: 1. Red rose extract with amla juice; 2. Red rose extract with baking soda solution; 3. Hydrangea in soil whose water turns the extract green; 4. Red rose extract with sugar solution
Column II: a. Red; b. Green; c. Colour unchanged; d. Pink or red flowers

A student prepares extract from fallen red rose petals. She adds it to a sample and sees red. Her friend says that the same sample will turn red litmus paper blue. Who is right about what litmus shows?
questions.a: Red with the extract means acidic (green means basic). An acid turns blue litmus red and leaves red litmus unchanged.
o: The friend is wrong: the sample is acidic, so blue litmus turns red and red litmus is unchanged
The friend is right: any sample that changes the extract also changes red litmus
The friend is wrong: the sample is neutral, so neither litmus paper changes colour
The friend is right: red in the extract means basic, and basic turns red litmus blue

questions.q:
The science club sets up four test tubes with red rose extract. Test tube A gets lemon juice, B soap solution, C tap water and D tamarind water. A visitor adds a liquid to a fifth test tube, and its extract turns green. The club must pick one indicator for the stall: blue litmus alone, or red rose extract.
(a) Give the colour in each of A, B, C and D.
(b) Which two test tubes look alike, and why?
(c) What is the visitor's liquid, in nature, and what would red litmus show?
(d) Which indicator should the club pick to separate acidic, basic and neutral liquids at a glance? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A red, B green, C unchanged, D red. (b) A and D, because both are acidic. (c) Basic; red litmus turns blue. (d) Red rose extract, since it gives three different results (red, green, no change). Blue litmus alone turns red only in acids and cannot separate basic from neutral liquids.
s: Part (a): red, green, unchanged, red
Part (b): A and D, both acidic
Part (c): basic, red litmus turns blue
Part (d): chooses extract, with three different results justified

questions.q: A village school has no litmus paper. Compare litmus and red rose extract as acid-base indicators and justify whether the school can safely use red rose extract instead.
questions.a: Litmus comes from lichens as solution or paper; red rose extract is prepared from petals. Litmus: blue paper turns red in acid, red paper turns blue in base. Rose extract: red in acid, green in base; both leave neutral substances unchanged. Both separate acidic, basic and neutral samples, so the school can use the extract after preparing it from fallen petals, since the book calls it another acid-base indicator.
s: Source of each indicator
Colours of litmus in acid and base
Colours of rose extract in acid and base
Both leave neutral substances unchanged
Justified decision: the school can use it

questions.q: Two hydrangea shrubs stand a few metres apart in the same hill garden, one with blue flowers and one with pink flowers. Give a reason for the difference and say what would have to change in the soil of the pink shrub for it to bear blue flowers.
questions.a: The soils differ: the blue shrub grows in acidic soil and the pink one in basic soil. The pink shrub's soil would have to become acidic.
s: Soil nature differs: acidic for blue, basic for pink
Pink shrub's soil must be made acidic

questions.q: Kabir plans his red rose extract: pluck a fistful of roses from the school garden, wash and crush the petals, immerse them in hot water in a tumbler, cover it for 5 to 10 minutes and filter. Which change does the chapter's activity require in his plan?
questions.a: The activity advises not to pluck flowers but to pick fallen petals; the other changes are not asked for (the filtrate, not the petals, is the extract).
o: Use petals that have fallen on the ground instead of plucking flowers
Boil the petals on a flame for an hour in place of using hot water
Skip the filtering and use the crushed petals as the indicator
Leave the covered tumbler untouched overnight rather than 5 to 10 minutes

questions.q: Aman has prepared red rose extract. He tests four samples: lemon juice, baking soda solution, salt solution and amla juice. Predict the colour for each, sort them into three groups and say what blue litmus would show for each group.
questions.a: Lemon juice and amla juice turn the extract red (acidic group); baking soda solution turns it green (basic group); salt solution leaves it unchanged (neutral group). Blue litmus turns red in the acidic group and does not change in the other two.
s: Lemon juice and amla juice red
Baking soda solution green
Salt solution no change
Correct grouping acidic / basic / neutral
Blue litmus: red only for the acidic group

questions.q:
Mrs Lepcha runs a nursery in Sikkim. Hydrangea flowers in bed A are blue and in bed B are pink. She shakes a soil sample from each bed in water, filters it and adds a few drops of red rose extract. Bed A's liquid shows red; bed B's liquid shows green. Bed C has weak plants, and its liquid leaves the extract unchanged.
(a) State the nature of the soil in beds A and B.
(b) She wants pink flowers in bed A. What should she add and why?
(c) What is the nature of bed C's soil?
(d) A helper wants to add lime to bed C. Decide whether this is sensible and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) A acidic, B basic. (b) Lime, a base, to neutralise the acid and make the soil less acidic. (c) Neutral. (d) No. The soil is already neutral, so lime will not cure the problem; the plants may lack nutrients, which she should check.
s: Part (a): A acidic, B basic
Part (b): lime, a base, neutralises acidic soil
Part (c): neutral
Part (d): lime not sensible, nutrient deficiency is likely

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Red rose extract is an acid-base indicator.
Reason (R): Hydrangea flowers are blue in acidic soil.
questions.a: Both are true, but the hydrangea colour does not explain why the extract is an indicator.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q:
The science club has 12 unlabelled bottles to sort into acidic, basic and neutral. It has a roll of turmeric paper and 20 strips of blue litmus. Bottle 1 turns turmeric paper red. Bottles 2 and 3 leave turmeric yellow; on blue litmus, bottle 2 turns red and bottle 3 does not change.
(a) State the nature of bottle 1.
(b) Can turmeric paper alone separate bottles 2 and 3? Why?
(c) State the nature of bottles 2 and 3.
(d) The club tests all 12 with turmeric first and uses blue litmus only on the bottles that stay yellow. If 5 bottles turn red, how many blue litmus strips are used, and is the plan sufficient?
questions.a: (a) Basic. (b) No: it stays yellow in both acidic and neutral liquids. (c) Bottle 2 acidic, bottle 3 neutral. (d) 12 - 5 = 7 strips, which is within the 20 available. The plan works and saves strips, but the 5 red bottles are only known to be basic, which is all the club needs.
s: Part (a): basic
Part (b): cannot, acidic and neutral both stay yellow
Part (c): acidic and neutral
Part (d): 7 strips, within 20, plan suffices

questions.q:
At the school fair stall 'Magic Pictures', Anaya draws a sun on white paper with a cotton bud dipped in liquid A and a moon with liquid B. After drying she sprays turmeric solution over the sheet. The sun appears red but the moon does not appear. She plans to spray red rose extract on a second sheet drawn the same way.
(a) What is the nature of liquid A?
(b) What can you say about liquid B?
(c) With red rose extract, what colour will the sun be, and what happens to the moon if B is acidic or if B is neutral?
(d) Anaya wants both pictures visible. Which paper should she use to test B first, and what should she do next?
questions.a: (a) Basic. (b) B is not basic; it is acidic or neutral. (c) The sun turns green; the moon turns red if B is acidic and does not show if B is neutral. (d) Test B with blue litmus: if it turns red, B is acidic and the extract spray will show both pictures; if it does not change, B is neutral and she should choose another liquid for the moon.
s: Part (a): basic
Part (b): acidic or neutral
Part (c): sun green; moon red or invisible
Part (d): blue litmus test, then decision on B

questions.q: Sneha gets two turmeric curry stains on a white shirt. She scrubs one with soap solution and dabs the other with lemon juice. The first stain turns reddish and the second stays yellow. What does this show?
questions.a: Turmeric turns red in basic solutions and stays yellow in acidic and neutral ones, so soap solution is basic while lemon juice (acidic) is not.
o: Soap solution is basic, and lemon juice is not basic
Soap solution is acidic, and lemon juice is basic
Both soap solution and lemon juice are neutral
Soap solution is neutral, and lemon juice is acidic only

questions.q: Tanvi places one drop each of lemon juice and tamarind water at the ends of a yellow turmeric paper strip and one drop of sugar solution in the middle. What does she see?
questions.a: Lemon juice and tamarind water are acidic and sugar solution is neutral; turmeric stays yellow in both.
o: No change anywhere; the strip stays yellow
Red at the lemon juice end only
Red at both ends
Red in the middle only

questions.q: Differentiate between turmeric paper and litmus paper on what they can detect.
questions.a: Litmus (blue and red) can show acidic and basic substances, so it classifies all three types. Turmeric paper turns red only in bases and cannot tell acidic from neutral substances.
s: Litmus detects both acids and bases
Turmeric detects only bases

questions.q: Neha plans to sort lime water, lemon juice and salt solution into acidic, basic and neutral groups using only turmeric paper. Explain the flaw in her plan.
questions.a: Lime water turns turmeric red. Lemon juice (acidic) and salt solution (neutral) both leave it yellow. She will get only two groups and needs a second indicator such as blue litmus.
s: Lime water turns it red
Lemon juice and salt solution look the same
Only two groups; a second indicator is needed

questions.q: Neha wants to find out whether lemon juice and soap solution change the odour of onion. Write her plan: how she prepares the strips, what she checks first, what she does next and how she records and concludes.
questions.a: Keep finely chopped onion with clean cotton or filter paper strips in a tightly closed container overnight. Smell two strips first. Put drops of lemon juice on one and soap solution on the other. Smell again and compare. Record the odour before and after in a table with the nature (acidic or basic) of each liquid; if the odour changes in an acid or a base, onion is acting as an olfactory indicator.
s: Onion with strips in a closed container overnight
Smell the strips before adding anything
Lemon juice on one strip, soap solution on the other
Smell again and compare
Record in a table and conclude about an olfactory indicator

questions.q: True or False: 'An olfactory indicator is a substance whose colour changes in an acidic or a basic medium, as turmeric does.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. An olfactory indicator is a substance whose odour (smell) changes in an acidic or basic medium, such as finely chopped onion. Turmeric changes colour, so it is a colour indicator.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: olfactory indicators change odour, not colour

questions.q: (a) One drop each of washing powder solution, vinegar and salt solution is put on three turmeric paper strips. State the colour of each strip. (b) How many of the three samples can turmeric paper single out, and which one?
questions.a: (a) Washing powder solution: red; vinegar: yellow; salt solution: yellow. (b) Only one, the washing powder solution (basic); the other two look alike.
s: (a) Red, yellow, yellow in that order
(b) Only the basic washing powder solution is singled out

questions.q: Rohit tests a clear liquid with turmeric paper and the paper stays yellow. He says: 'So the liquid is acidic.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. Turmeric paper stays yellow in acidic and in neutral solutions, so a yellow result only shows the liquid is not basic. He would need blue litmus or red rose extract to decide.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Yellow occurs in both acidic and neutral liquids
Another indicator (blue litmus or extract) is needed to decide

questions.q: Meera paints a message with lime water on dried turmeric paper, and Dev paints his with lemon juice on another sheet. Which message becomes visible?
questions.a: Lime water is basic, so turmeric turns red where it is applied. Lemon juice is acidic, so the paper stays yellow.
o: Only Meera's, as red writing on yellow
Only Dev's, as red writing on yellow
Both, as red writing
Neither, because turmeric paper changes only in a neutral liquid

questions.q: A strip of turmeric paper turns red when a clear liquid falls on it. State what you can conclude about the liquid, what you cannot conclude, and name one further test that narrows it down, with the result you would expect.
questions.a: The liquid is basic. It cannot be named exactly (soap solution, lime water and baking soda solution all do this). Red litmus would turn blue, or red rose extract would turn green.
s: The liquid is basic
Cannot say which basic liquid it is
A further test with its expected result

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A drop of soap solution turns turmeric paper red; 2. A drop of lemon juice leaves turmeric paper yellow; 3. Chopped onion strips smell different after baking soda solution is put on them; 4. Turmeric paper gives the same yellow with vinegar and with sugar solution
Column II: a. The liquid is basic; b. The liquid is not basic (acidic or neutral); c. Onion is behaving as an olfactory indicator; d. Turmeric paper cannot tell these two apart

(a) Finely chopped onion and clean cotton strips are kept overnight in a tightly closed container. A few drops of baking soda solution on one strip change its odour. What does this show about onion and about baking soda solution? (b) Which step must be done before adding any drop, and why?
questions.a: (a) Onion works as an olfactory indicator, and the change in odour shows the medium is basic (baking soda solution is a base). (b) Smell the strip first, so that the odour before and after adding the drop can be compared.
s: (a) Onion is an olfactory indicator; baking soda solution is basic
(b) Smell before the drop so that a comparison is possible

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Turmeric paper turns red in soap solution.
Reason (R): Turmeric is a member of the ginger family.
questions.a: Both are true, but the plant family of turmeric does not explain the colour change; the paper turns red because soap solution is basic.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Turmeric paper turns red in a basic solution.
2. Turmeric paper can tell vinegar from sugar solution.
3. Turmeric paper stays yellow only in acidic solutions.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is true. 2 is false (both stay yellow) and 3 is false (it also stays yellow in neutral solutions).
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: On three strips of turmeric paper a student places a drop of lime water, a drop of vinegar and a drop of tap water. The number of strips that turn red is ___.

Sita keeps chopped onion with filter paper strips in a closed box overnight and smells two strips. She then puts a few drops of tamarind water on one strip and baking soda solution on the other. Which observation would show onion acting as an olfactory indicator?
questions.a: An olfactory indicator is a substance whose odour changes in an acidic or basic medium, so the test is a change of smell, not of colour.
o: The odour of a strip is different after the drops than before
A strip turns red where the baking soda solution falls
The odour of both strips stays exactly the same after the drops
The strips turn blue where the tamarind water falls

questions.q: Samples: lime water, vinegar and sugar solution. Indicators: red litmus, turmeric paper and red rose extract. Write the result of each indicator for each sample and state which indicator alone can separate all three samples.
questions.a: Lime water: red litmus turns blue, turmeric turns red, extract green. Vinegar: red litmus no change, turmeric yellow, extract red. Sugar solution: no change, yellow, no change. Red litmus and turmeric each give the same result for vinegar and sugar solution. Only red rose extract gives three different results.
s: Lime water row correct
Vinegar row correct
Sugar solution row correct
Red litmus and turmeric cannot separate vinegar from sugar solution
Red rose extract alone separates all three

questions.q: After their turmeric-paper tests, four teams write conclusions. Which team's conclusion is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Yellow turmeric paper only shows a liquid is not basic. Tamarind water is acidic and neutrality is not shown by this test, so Team D's conclusion goes too far.
o: Team D: it stayed yellow in tamarind water, so tamarind water is neutral
Team A: it stayed yellow in lemon juice, so lemon juice is not basic
Team B: it turned red in lime water, so lime water is basic
Team C: it stayed yellow in salt solution, so salt solution is not basic

questions.q: A white cloth is dipped in turmeric paste and dried. A drop of lime water falls on one spot and a drop of tap water on another. Predict what happens at each spot and why.
questions.a: The lime water spot turns red because lime water is basic; the tap water spot stays yellow because tap water is neutral.
s: Lime water spot red, since it is basic
Tap water spot stays yellow, since it is neutral

questions.q: Dipak adds lime water to lemon juice with blue litmus solution until it has only just turned blue. He then adds one more drop of lemon juice. What will he see?
questions.a: The extra acid makes the mixture acidic again, so the litmus turns red.
o: The solution turns red again
The solution stays blue permanently
The solution turns colourless
The solution turns green

questions.q: True or False: 'A thermometer in lemon juice reads 28 degrees C. After enough lime water is mixed in to neutralise it, the reading should be above 28 degrees C.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Neutralisation is acid + base giving salt + water + heat, so heat is released and the temperature of the mixture rises.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: neutralisation releases heat

questions.q: Dev has vinegar, blue litmus solution and washing powder solution. Describe how he can show neutralisation, stating the colour at each stage and what is formed.
questions.a: Put vinegar with water in a test tube and add blue litmus; it turns red. Add washing powder solution slowly and swirl. When enough is added the colour changes from red to blue, so the vinegar is no longer acidic. Salt and water are formed with release of heat. One more drop of vinegar then makes it acidic and red again.
s: Vinegar with blue litmus gives red
Washing powder solution added slowly with swirling
Red changes to blue: no longer acidic
Salt and water formed with heat released
Extra vinegar turns it red again

questions.q:
Sanjana mixes lemon juice with lime water in beaker 1. A thermometer reads 28 degrees C before and 31 degrees C after, and the final liquid leaves both red and blue litmus unchanged. In beaker 2 she keeps adding lime water past beaker 1's stage, and the liquid turns red litmus blue.
(a) By how many degrees did the temperature rise, and which part of the equation does this match?
(b) What is the nature of the liquid in beaker 1?
(c) Why does beaker 2 turn red litmus blue?
(d) She wants a neutral liquid for disposal. Which beaker is suitable, and how can she correct the other?
questions.a: (a) 3 degrees C; heat released. (b) Neutral. (c) The excess lime water makes it basic. (d) Beaker 1; for beaker 2 add lemon juice a little at a time until red litmus stops turning blue.
s: Part (a): 3 degrees C rise, heat term
Part (b): neutral
Part (c): excess base makes it basic
Part (d): beaker 1, and acid added a little at a time to beaker 2

questions.q: After enough lime water is added to lemon juice, neither litmus paper changes colour. Explain why.
questions.a: The acid has been neutralised by the base, so the solution is neither acidic nor basic and cannot change either litmus paper.
s: Acid neutralised by the base
Neither acidic nor basic, so no litmus change

questions.q: A student says: 'Adding any amount of base to an acid makes the solution neutral.' Justify whether this is correct, using Activity 2.7.
questions.a: Not correct; the amount matters. With too little lime water the solution is still acidic and blue litmus stays red. When enough is added the solution is neither acidic nor basic. If a lot more lime water is added the solution turns basic and red litmus turns blue. In the activity the blue colour appears only after sufficient lime water. So only a sufficient quantity neutralises.
s: Too little base: still acidic, litmus red
Sufficient base: neither acidic nor basic
Excess base leaves a basic solution
Activity 2.7 shows blue only after enough lime water
Conclusion: any amount does not work

questions.q: In a neutralisation test the thermometer reads 29 degrees C before mixing and 34 degrees C after. The heat released raised the temperature by ___ degrees C.

A student adds lime water drop by drop to lemon juice containing blue litmus solution. After 10 drops the mixture is still red; after 18 drops it first turns blue. (a) What is the nature of the mixture after 10 drops, and why? (b) She adds 10 more drops after it has turned blue. Predict the colour and the nature of the mixture.
questions.a: (a) Acidic, because not enough base has been added yet to neutralise the acid. (b) It stays blue; the extra base makes the mixture basic.
s: (a) Still acidic: too little base added
(b) Stays blue; the excess base makes it basic

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The test tube becomes warm when lemon juice is neutralised by lime water.
Reason (R): Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water.
questions.a: Both are true, but the composition of lime water does not explain the warmth; the heat is released by the neutralisation reaction.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q: Ila says that adding water to lemon juice neutralises it because the juice becomes weaker. Jai says that neutralisation needs an acid and a base. (a) Who is right? (b) Name the two substances and the form of energy that are formed or released along with each other in true neutralisation.
questions.a: (a) Jai. Blue litmus solution still turns red in lemon juice diluted with about twenty drops of water, so the diluted juice is still acidic. (b) Salt and water are formed and heat is released.
s: (a) Jai is right; diluted lemon juice still turns blue litmus solution red
(b) Salt and water formed, heat released

questions.q: Tara mixes an acid and a base. The mixture changes neither red nor blue litmus paper. This shows that
questions.a: Neutralisation gives a solution that is neither acidic nor basic.
o: it is neither acidic nor basic
the acid is still present in excess
the base is still present in excess
no reaction has taken place

questions.q:
Kabir puts 5 mL of lemon juice solution in a test tube with a few drops of blue litmus solution. He adds lime water one drop at a time (about 20 drops make 1 mL), swirling. After 20 drops it is still red; after 35 drops it is blue. The test tube is slightly warm. Zoya suggests adding 2 mL at once next time to save time.
(a) What does the blue colour at 35 drops show?
(b) Why is the test tube warm?
(c) Two more drops of lemon juice are added at 35 drops. What happens to the colour?
(d) How many drops is 2 mL, how does it compare with 35, and should Kabir follow Zoya's plan?
questions.a: (a) The acid has been neutralised. (b) Neutralisation releases heat. (c) It turns red again. (d) 2 mL is 40 drops, 5 more than the 35 needed, so the extra base would leave the solution basic; drop by drop is better when the aim is a neutral solution.
s: Part (a): acid neutralised
Part (b): heat released
Part (c): turns red again
Part (d): 40 drops, 5 extra, excess base, so drop by drop

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. In a neutralisation reaction salt and water are formed with release of heat.
2. An acid and a base mixed in sufficient quantity give a solution that is neither acidic nor basic.
3. Lemon juice with blue litmus solution is red, and it turns blue when enough lime water is added.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are true and are taken from the chapter.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Match each stage of Activity 2.7 in Column I with what happens or what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. Lemon juice with a drop of blue litmus solution; 2. Lime water added until the colour changes from red to blue; 3. The test tube feels warm to the hand; 4. One more drop of lemon juice after the blue stage
Column II: a. Heat is released in neutralisation; b. The solution is red, so it is acidic; c. The solution is no longer acidic; d. The colour goes back to red because the solution turns acidic again
A teacher mixes equal volumes of two clear liquids in four test tubes. In which tube will the students feel warmth that comes from neutralisation?
questions.a: Warmth from neutralisation needs an acid reacting with a base. Lemon juice is acidic and lime water is basic. The other pairs are two acids or two neutral liquids.
o: Lemon juice and lime water
Lemon juice and vinegar
Sugar solution and salt solution
Tap water and sugar solution

questions.q: Lemon juice and enough lime water are mixed until neither litmus paper changes colour. The mixture holds something that was in neither starting liquid. What is it?
questions.a: Neutralisation forms salt and water with heat; a salt is the new substance. Chuna is used only to prepare lime water, and formic acid is the red ant's acid.
o: A salt
Chuna (calcium oxide)
A stronger acid
Formic acid

questions.q:
(a) Write the word equation for neutralisation.
(b) A test tube feels warm when an acid is mixed with a base. Which part of the equation explains this?
questions.a: (a) Acid + Base -> Salt + Water + Heat. (b) The heat term: heat is released.
s: Part (a): equation correct
Part (b): heat released

questions.q: Neha says: 'In neutralisation only water is formed.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly. Water is formed, but so are a salt and heat: acid + base gives salt + water + heat.
s: Verdict: partly right
Water is formed but a salt is also formed
Heat is released

questions.q:
(a) Vinegar is mixed with lime water in sufficient quantity. Name what is formed.
(b) What will blue litmus and red litmus show with the final mixture?
questions.a: (a) Salt and water, with heat released. (b) Neither paper changes colour, because the mixture is neither acidic nor basic.
s: Part (a): salt and water with heat
Part (b): no change on either litmus paper

questions.q: Two clear liquids are mixed in a test tube. The tube becomes warm and the final liquid changes neither red nor blue litmus. Describe what the two liquids could have been and what happened.
questions.a: One liquid was an acid and the other a base (for example lemon juice and lime water) mixed in sufficient quantity. They neutralised each other, forming salt and water and releasing heat, so the result is neutral.
s: One acidic and one basic liquid
Neutralisation forming salt and water
Heat released, result neither acidic nor basic

questions.q: Show that adding vinegar to lemon juice cannot neutralise the lemon juice.
questions.a: Both vinegar and lemon juice are acidic (they turn blue litmus red). Neutralisation needs an acid and a base, so mixing two acids leaves the solution acidic.
s: Both are acidic
Neutralisation needs an acid and a base
Mixture stays acidic

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Excess use of chemical fertilisers can make soil acidic.
Reason (R): Lime is a base.
questions.a: Both are true, but lime being a base does not explain why fertilisers make soil acidic.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q: A factory beside a lake releases acidic waste and the fish are declining. (a) Name the process the factory can use before releasing the waste and what it must add. (b) A trial batch with too much of the added substance turns red litmus blue. Is it neutral? Say what it is.
questions.a: (a) Neutralisation, by adding a basic substance to the waste. (b) No; it is basic, because the added base is in excess.
s: (a) Neutralisation with a basic substance
(b) Not neutral; the excess base makes it basic

questions.q: A red ant bites Keerthi's hand. Two remedies are offered: moist baking soda or a few drops of vinegar. (a) Which should be used? (b) Name the liquid the ant injects and say why the other remedy is wrong.
questions.a: (a) Moist baking soda. (b) The ant injects formic acid, which a base neutralises; vinegar is itself an acid, so it cannot neutralise the sting.
s: (a) Moist baking soda, a base
(b) Formic acid; vinegar is an acid and cannot neutralise it

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Excess use of chemical fertilisers can make soil acidic.
2. Acidic factory waste can be neutralised by adding basic substances before release.
3. A neutral soil always gives healthy plants.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are true. 3 is false: neutral soil can still lack nutrients.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Four farmers explain what they found on their land. Whose explanation does the chapter NOT support?
questions.a: An unchanged extract means the soil is neutral, not acidic. The other three statements follow from the chapter.
o: Farmer W: soil water leaves red rose extract unchanged, so my sickly plants must be growing in acidic soil
Farmer X: I used too much chemical fertiliser, which can make my soil acidic, so I will add lime
Farmer Y: my soil is basic, so I will add manure, which releases acids that neutralise it
Farmer Z: my soil is neutral, but nutrient deficiency could still be making my plants unhealthy

questions.q: A farmer tests his soil with red rose extract and the extract turns green. His plants are growing poorly. What should he add?
questions.a: Green means basic soil. Organic matter releases acids that neutralise it. Lime and washing powder solution are bases and make it worse.
o: Manure and composted leaves
Lime
Washing powder solution
Nothing, because basic soil is always healthy

questions.q:
A factory near a lake releases acidic waste and the fish in the lake are declining. The factory adds a basic substance to the waste in three trial batches. Batch 1 still turns blue litmus red. Batch 2 changes neither litmus paper. Batch 3 turns red litmus blue.
(a) What does the result of batch 1 show?
(b) What does the result of batch 2 show?
(c) What does the result of batch 3 show?
(d) The engineer wants to use the batch 3 dose to be safe. Which batch dose should the factory adopt, and why?
questions.a: (a) Still acidic: not enough base added. (b) Neutral: the acid has been neutralised. (c) Basic: too much base added. (d) The batch 2 dose, because it gives a neutral waste; batch 3 only replaces an acidic waste by a basic one.
s: Part (a): still acidic
Part (b): neutral
Part (c): basic, too much base
Part (d): batch 2 dose, since it is neutral

questions.q: Differentiate the treatment of acidic soil from that of basic soil, naming the substance used and how it acts in each case.
questions.a: Acidic soil is treated with lime, a base, which neutralises the acid. Basic soil is treated with manure or composted leaves, which release acids that neutralise the base.
s: Acidic soil: lime, a base, neutralises the acid
Basic soil: manure or composted leaves release acids that neutralise it

questions.q: Four situations from the chapter involve neutralisation: a red ant bite, acidic soil, basic soil and acidic factory waste. For each, state which of acid or base is the problem and the remedy.
questions.a: Ant bite: acid (formic acid), remedy moist baking soda. Acidic soil: remedy lime, a base. Basic soil: remedy manure or composted leaves, which release acids. Acidic factory waste: remedy a basic substance before release. In each, the opposite kind of substance cancels the problem.
s: Ant bite: acid, baking soda
Acidic soil: lime
Basic soil: organic matter
Factory waste: basic substance
Common idea: the opposite kind cancels the problem

questions.q: Lime costs Rs 30 per kg. A garden plot with acidic soil needs 2.5 kg of it, so the lime will cost Rs ___.

Match each observation in Column I with the step in Column II.
Column I: 1. Soil water turns red rose extract red; 2. Soil water turns red litmus paper blue; 3. Soil water leaves the extract unchanged but the plants are weak; 4. A stinging red patch appears after an ant bite

(a) Why do plants grow poorly in a field where chemical fertiliser has been used in excess?
(b) What is added to treat it?
questions.a: (a) The excess makes the soil acidic. (b) Lime, a base.
s: Part (a): soil becomes acidic
Part (b): lime, a base

questions.q: True or False: 'Plants can grow poorly in a farmer's soil even when soil water leaves red rose extract unchanged.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Unchanged extract means the soil is neutral, but a neutral soil can still lack nutrients, which makes the plants unhealthy.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: neutral soil may have a deficiency of nutrients

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Moist baking soda gives relief from a red ant bite.
Reason (R): The ant injects formic acid, which the baking soda, a base, neutralises.
questions.a: Both are true and the neutralisation of the acid explains the relief.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.

questions.q: The soil water of a garden bed leaves red rose extract unchanged, yet its plants are weak and yellowing. What is the most likely reason?
questions.a: An unchanged extract means neutral soil; weak plants in neutral soil may be due to nutrient deficiency.
o: The soil lacks nutrients
The soil is acidic
The soil is basic
Too much lime was added

questions.q: Show that adding lime to soil that is already basic cannot help the plants.
questions.a: Lime is a base. Adding a base to a basic soil makes it more basic; only an acid-releasing material like manure can neutralise it.
s: Lime is a base
Base added to basic soil makes it more basic
Neutralising needs acid-releasing organic matter

questions.q: A farmer tests soil water from three plots. Plot P turns blue litmus paper red, plot Q turns red litmus paper blue, and plot R leaves both papers unchanged. He has one bag of lime. Where should it go?
questions.a: Blue litmus turning red shows plot P is acidic, and lime is a base. Plot Q is already basic and plot R is neutral, so lime would not help either.
o: Plot P only
Plot Q only
Plot R only
All three plots equally

questions.q: Rahul says: 'A few drops of vinegar rubbed on a red ant bite will relieve the pain, because the sting is sour and vinegar is sour too.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The ant injects an acid (formic acid) and vinegar is also acidic. Relief needs a base, such as moist baking soda, to neutralise the acid; adding another acid does not do that.
s: Verdict: disagrees
The sting is an acid and vinegar is acidic too
A base such as moist baking soda neutralises it

questions.q: A farmer found his soil acidic and added a large quantity of lime. Next season his plants are poor again and the soil turns red litmus blue. Explain what went wrong, how to correct it and what he should do in future.
questions.a: Lime is a base. Too much lime neutralised the acid and left the soil basic, so red litmus turns blue. Basic soil is treated by adding organic matter such as manure and composted leaves, which release acids. In future he should test the soil with an indicator and add lime only as needed.
s: Lime is a base, so excess makes the soil basic
The red litmus result shows basic soil
Treat with manure or composted leaves
Organic matter releases acids
Test with an indicator before treating

questions.q: Describe a soil situation in which adding manure is the right step. Say what the soil test would show before and after.
questions.a: The soil is basic: red litmus turns blue (or red rose extract turns green). Manure and composted leaves release acids that neutralise it, so after treatment the soil is less basic.
s: Soil is basic
Test result before treatment
Organic matter releases acids that neutralise it

questions.q:
The school garden has three plots. Soil water from plot P turns red rose extract red, from plot Q green, and from plot R leaves it unchanged, but plants in R are weak. Mr Reddy has a budget of Rs 100. Lime costs Rs 24 per kg and plot P needs 3 kg. Composted leaves from the school compost pit are free.
(a) State the nature of the soil in P, Q and R.
(b) What should be used on P and on Q?
(c) How much will the lime for P cost?
(d) Decide how he should use the rest of the money for plot R, and why not lime.
questions.a: (a) P acidic, Q basic, R neutral. (b) P: lime; Q: composted leaves. (c) 3 x 24 = Rs 72. (d) Rs 28 remain; R is neutral so lime or leaves will not cure it; he should check for nutrient deficiency and use the remaining money on nutrients for R.
s: Part (a): acidic, basic, neutral
Part (b): lime for P, composted leaves for Q
Part (c): Rs 72
Part (d): Rs 28 left, check nutrients, not lime
